utterances.text: Yes. And all I can say is that there were also rifles and ammunition from municipal staffs of the Territorial Defence. From Sokolac, Han Pijesak, two Sarajevo municipalities, I think. Novo Sarajevo or Novi Grad and the municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. What different types of rifles did you have for distribution to VRS forces? You've told us about the 7.9 calibre rifle. What else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the reserve I only had M-48 7.9 rifles, and I think they were M-47s.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "in the reserve" were those rifles for distribution to VRS forces or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of the war, that is to say in the second year, instead of defective rifles, 7.62, semi-automatic or automatic ones, M-48s were issued, M-48 rifles were issued in accordance with the orders from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about towards the beginning and the middle of the war, did you distribute to rifles to the forces of the VRS? Was that part of your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main duties involved issuing ammunition and mines and ordnance. That was the purpose of my warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am not asking you about ammunition. Did you or did you not issue rifles to VRS forces before August 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't issue any, apart from M-48, 7.9 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we have a problem in the transcript. I heard something being said to Mr. Ierace and this isn't in the transcript. I think that Mr. -- Transcript said and I can't find that in the transcript any more. I don't know. Was something skipped? I am quite sure that I heard Mr. Ierace say this sentence which can't be found in the transcript. I am raising this question as a matter of principle because everything should be included in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there is no disagreement on the principle. Even though it says "Mr. Transcript said something" which is quite surprising but I know that the transcribers are doing their utmost best to reflect every single word. It is not my recollection that anything is missing. If Mr. Ierace finds anything missing, please inform us, if not, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you can listen to the tapes at a later stage tell the court what exactly you are missing. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What about machine-guns before 1994, month of August, did you distribute any machine-guns to VRS forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I didn't have such weapons in the warehouse, apart from the staffs of the Territorial Defence, weapons that they had taken. And I said that as part of the reserve supplies, I only had the M-48, 7.9 rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that in that answer that I took you to, you were referring to the weaponry which the SRK had. When you referred to the domestic sniper rifle, were you referring to the M-76?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown a document. Mr. President, this will be P3769. Perhaps that could be placed on the ELMO. And perhaps we could see in particular the rifle in the bottom left-hand corner, if that could be centred, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you see on the bottom left-hand corner of the page in front of you a photograph of the M-76?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is it the position that when you joined the SRK you saw some of these rifles within the SRK; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. In the records, in the operative records that were there, such rifles weren't listed, but units did send them to be repaired in the workshop. The first time I saw such a rifle, as far as I can remember, was in -- when it was being repaired in a workshop. But there weren't many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you first see them, when did you first see such a rifle being repaired in a workshop? What year was that and what month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in 1993, but I can't remember when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And was that a rifle which had come from the SRK for repairs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When did you next see such a rifle from the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see such a rifle after that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So are you saying -- well, was that the only occasion that you saw such a rifle in the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Earlier you said in response to a question which related to when you joined the SRK and these rifles, "in the records, in the operative records that were there, such rifles weren't listed." When you joined the SRK, did you see any mention of such rifles in the records?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So you didn't -- the only time you ever saw one of these rifles during the war was sometime in 1993 being repaired, and whilst you were in the SRK, you never saw any record of such rifles. Did you see any record of such rifles anywhere else during the war? Any other VRS documentation of such rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see this in the records and similarly, I didn't see them where I went to carry out controls. I know that such weapons were fairly modern weapons. They had been recently produced. And I know that when they were being distributed, A-formation units would be given priority and then Territorial Defence units would buy those weapons themselves. So whether it had been included in all units, I couldn't really say, whether all units had them, I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And yet you provided ammunition for that particular rifle, is that correct, from the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such ammunition was distributed but it can also be used for an ordinary M-47 and M-48 rifles and for light machine-guns and for 7.9 millimetre machine-guns. The bullet is the same and they can be used for these weapons too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But, sir, didn't you stock special sniper bullets marked as such on the box as bullet for the sniper rifle 7.9 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? I didn't understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will read it back to you: "But, sir, didn't you stock special sniper bullets marked as such on the box as bullet for the sniper rifle 7.9 millimetre?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I stated. I said that such a bullet did exist and that this was marked on the case, and that on the whole the difference had to do with the charge, the way it was charged, in order to extend the range or rather make its trajectory more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What particular machine-guns were able to fire those bullets, the bullets in those particular boxes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a 7.9 millimetre rifle could do so, an M-48, then a light machine-gun, an M-53 light machine-gun, and a 7.9 millimetre machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see any 7.9 machine-guns in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you mention it in that particular paragraph that I asked you about earlier on page 21?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a light machine-gun, and a machine-gun are mentioned. It says the same and that means an M-53.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is an M-53 7.9 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is there any other weapon that you mentioned there, apart from the sniper rifle, which is 7.9 millimetres? Please check it, if you like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, those were 7.9 millimetre rifles. And then we had a light machine-gun, and a machine-gun, 7.9 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Haven't you mentioned only two weapons that could fire the 7.9? One is the machine-gun M-53, and the other is the M-76 sniper rifle; isn't that correct? They are the only two you've mentioned; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned speaking of calibres, 7.9 millimetre rifles. Further on, I mentioned a light machine-gun, machine-gun M-53, and the sniper rifles, 7.9 of domestic production.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right, now, you mentioned old rifles, 7.2, 7.9, being German rifles from World War II; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such rifles. There were M-47 or 49. I don't remember all the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did the M-53 machine-gun take belt ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And do you have -- I am sorry -- did you have belt ammunition for it in your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would it be a waste and also inefficient to use specialist sniper bullets loaded one by one into a machine-gun, when you have belt ammunition available, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that, but you can also load it. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, how much time would you still need? You said a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I didn't anticipate these answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that still does not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be finished by half past 12.00, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please try to finish in 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidently, did you join the SRK in January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of January, 28th or 29th of January, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. At the beginning of the war, how many tons of ammunition were in your warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly say exactly how much, but I think that there was some 7.000 tons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you joined the SRK in late January 1995, I take it that by then the artillery and the large mortars were under UN observation in various compounds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly because this obligation was carried out by the chief of artillery in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, but didn't you tell the investigator --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object in order to gain time, I hope. We are here speaking about the year 1995, which goes well beyond the time frame of the indictment. Perhaps the Prosecution could explain why they are walking out, stepping out of this time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace could you tell us what the relevance is of questions about --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it is difficult to do so in the presence of the witness. I can't do it in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom for...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you may proceed. We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please turn to page 27 of the transcript in Croatian, Bosnian and Serb. I direct your attention to the two paragraphs preceding the end of tape 2. In the question alongside the initials "MBTU" you were asked about sniper rifles and the SRK. Would you please read your answer. Before you do so I should say that you were asked also how many such rifles you would expect does this apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if you are referring to page 27 of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My apologies. It is 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I see that you are referring to page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Page 26, the two paragraphs before the end of tape 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can Mr. Ierace tell us what is the paragraph in Serbian so that we can save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think we have just done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 26. Just the last two paragraphs before the end of tape 2, side 1. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will repeat the question: In the first of those two paragraphs you were asked about the number of sniper rifles you would expect a corps the size of the SRK to be supplied. How many such sniper rifles would be supplied to such a corps. Would you now please read your answer, slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Let me tell you, I don't know that and I wouldn't" -- the translation is not good. I will try. "Let me tell you, I don't know that because I don't know how many such rifles there were at the beginning, sniper rifles, until when I got to the corps. Later on, there were so many rifles that were malfunctioning that they could no longer be used. That is why they were not maintained as they should have been."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, when you joined the corps, how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President, because we are doing this, we are coming back to ask the question about the time frame which is not included. Because we know that the witness joined the corps outside of the time frame of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's exactly the same problem as earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- could you give us some more information about the malfunctioning of these rifles. I understand that you were referring to sniper rifles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This answer, I was thinking about all weapons in general, all infantry weapons mostly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you were specifically asked about sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I said that in the records that I inherited, these rifles were not listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you are talking about the bad maintenance of these rifles. Could you tell us anything about the maintenance then specifically of the sniper rifles you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was speaking about the maintenance I said that in the use of the weapons while the weapons were used, they were not cleaned on a regular basis because of combat operations and because of the conditions of preservation, that is they were always outside in the open, exposed to the weather conditions. And it is possible that there was a lack of discipline of certain individuals. And also shall we say the way that certain individuals, their expertise or the lack of the expertise of the people who commanded their use, people who were in charge of units. All of this influenced the maintenance of the weapons and whether they were in working order or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I was specifically asking about sniper rifles. Could you give us -- you are talking general terms, how many malfunctioning sniper rifles you saw at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in 1993 it was the first time that I saw such a rifle being repaired in the workshop, and there was a problem with the optical sight, as far as I recall. The workmen from the Zrak factory who used to work in Sarajevo before, they had a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I asked about what you saw in 1995, but since your answer about malfunctioning of rifles was when you entered the SRK, how many malfunctioning sniper rifles did you see at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't seen them. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes your answer given in the transcript not easy to understand. Specifically asked in respect of sniper rifles, your answer starts with mentioning sniper rifles, and then you further explain that many rifles were out of order, which one would easily understand as to refer at least also to sniper rifles. Did you hear anything about malfunctioning sniper rifles, even if you might not have seen them yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear anything in particular, except for what I said, that the precision and the time that these rifles lasted, that this could have been influenced by the fact that they were not properly maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are now talking about these rifles, are you referring to sniper rifles as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, but I am telling you that I didn't have a record, precise exact record, how many of these rifles there were in the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, who was it that told you about problems with maintenance of sniper rifles within the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention anywhere nor did anyone speak to me about these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just tell us clearly, did you or did you not hear that there were maintenance problems with the sniper rifles in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no problems. I haven't heard that there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. So the situation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We now won't have any more time. The witness, who is going to have to come back in January, and I am just saying this as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes facts do not seem to be as they are. I asked whether we would have additional time available today to sit. I hope that I will be informed about it soon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, obviously the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17114 to 17130. facts, they do not seem to be as they are. We already organised a visit in the Detention Unit this afternoon. We are taken -- our agenda is full. This is the first time or the last time that we are able to see General Galic before the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: A minute or two, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, so I can understand what you are telling us about sniper rifles, is this the position: During the war you only ever saw one. You understood that the SRK had them, as we see in the transcript, but apart from that one you didn't see them, you never saw any records about them, and you never heard any problems about maintenance or malfunctioning of these weapons. Have I accurately summarised your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As the parties might be aware of, the Chamber tries to prepare a continuation later this afternoon, but of course a lot of arrangements has to be made, if we would be able to finish, that of course would have been far better. So I call upon the parties to work as efficiently as possible and we certainly would finish with this witness before the lunch break. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. I haven't asked yet, but is there any need on the side of the Defence to re-examine the witness? I take it that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear that last -- but

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, first of all, good afternoon. You answered to a question asked earlier in relation to the sniper rifle, as we call it, and to units. My question is the following: If each unit had received a delivery of these so-called sniper rifles, that would have been found in the records that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I also had one additional question that just occurred to me, and this one is in relation to the ammunition, the so-called incendiary ammunition. Do you know if infantry troops of the corps had such ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. There is no reference to time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Whatever the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace, I think if we need clarification, we would ask for it, as far as the time is concerned. We are talking about the -- when you were in charge of the warehouse, could you answer the question in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when the ammunition was issued for the semi-automatic machine-guns, that's how it was packed. The ammunition was packed in cartridge belts, an ordinary bullet, anti-armour bullet, incendiary bullet, that's how it was issued. It was issued in packages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am speaking -- perhaps that was not properly interpreted -- but I am speaking about infantry troops. My question was in relation to infantry troops.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know among infantry troops there were anti-aircraft machine-guns, according to the establishment structure that they were supposed to have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP30, you told us about the warehouses and where they were. You also told us about the Marshal Tito Barracks in Sarajevo. Were there any warehouses apart from storage in Marshal Tito Barracks, were there any warehouse that were after the encirclement of Sarajevo, at least, well, troops gathering around Sarajevo. So after the lines had been established, were there any warehouses within the, I would say, the BiH-held part of the city or were they all in the Republika Srpska-held territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo itself, I can't be very precise about that because there were a number of barracks there, for example, Viktor Bubanj, Jusuf Dzonlic, the barracks at Alipasino and then in Nedzarici, Rajlovac, the school centre, there was a command at Bistrik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not asking about -- but specialised warehouses where greater amounts of ammunition and/or weaponry was stored. You told us about Faletici and how it went with Faletici. But similar warehouses of similar size, were they also within the BiH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know there weren't -- there wasn't such big warehouse in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Then you told us that the JNA was standing guard at the Faletici warehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the guard of some units from Lukavica was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that normal that the JNA would stand guard at what, if I understood your testimony well, was a TO, Territorial Defence warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was normal, because they didn't have men who were permanently mobilised and who could stand guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So JNA had some -- there was JNA presence where the TO would have stored its weapons, is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that by the warehouse of the Territorial Defence there were reserve units which were part of the JNA. There was probably some equipment belonged to some units from Lukavica that had been stored there or what I mentioned earlier on while I worked in Zenica, there was a ABH (nuclear, biological, chemical) battalion, a reserve force battalion, so I don't know exactly what else there was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Mr. DP30, let me first ask, I do understand, Mr. Ierace, that a further -- that you do not tender that part of the transcript which has not been reviewed by the witness. Is that a correct understanding? These are the last -- I think it is on from page 30. Would be 30, 31, 32 and a few lines on 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will rely on that, but given the requirements of the Trial Chamber for the tender of a record of that part of the interview, in my submission that would provide a proper basis for having been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and of course we do not have any explanations and clarifications as we had on the other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: However, the steps to be taken should resolve any difficulties with the interpretation provided by the field interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the indication the Chamber has given is an indication including page 29, and we have to see what happens if you will tender, finally, the last pages. Then may I ask you -- Mr. DP30, I would like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I thank you for -- yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I draw your attention to one aspect of those pages, page 32, almost halfway down the page, indeed the first question asked on that page which is the second paragraph, there is an issue there which I think is relevant to these proceedings. If you are minded, because the witness has not checked it, to decline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that page 32?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is the second answer on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The first question on that page raises an issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the first question, that is the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have spoken about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that is an important issue for these proceedings and I would have no objection if you, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will read it to the witness and see whether there is any comments. Mr. DP30, I will read two passages of the part that you might not have checked, because it might be of importance, because the Prosecution thinks it is of importance. I will read it to you and if there is any comment to be made on the correctness of the answer or whether you said this or not, please let me know. The question was at that time: "We've spoken about ammunition that was supplied, that was manufactured within the Republika Srpska. Did you receive ammunition from any other sources?" And then the transcript reads as your answer: "As far as I know, ammunition was also supplied from the production from Yugoslavia because we sent our vehicles, we sent our vehicles to Cacak and Kragujevac. I don't know which other places because there was another officer who was in charge for that, and of course, that was ordered by the Ministry of Defence. And I know that we were receiving invoices for the -- for the certain things that should be authorised by us in the base because we had to certify that we really received it, otherwise that could be paid." Is this -- apart from the language, perhaps not always been very clear, but the main part is that you also received ammunition produced in Yugoslavia and that invoices were sent for that. Is that reflecting what you said at that time and is there any comment that you would like to make on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to say that we didn't receive it, but we bought it. Perhaps the translation is not correct. We obtained this through the Ministry of Defence. And when we received this ammunition, then it was necessary to compile a document which then had to be certified so that the Ministry of Defence could make the necessary payment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand that this was delivery upon payment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President I don't require that the questions and answers in relation to that issue be read except for one sentence and it is convenient for you perhaps I would read it out to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This appears about two-thirds of the way down the page, halfway through an answer purportedly given by the witness. "Before I left for the" --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. This will be the third time that we will be returning to the -- this issue. I think that the Prosecution had the time to do this. It has taken more time to ask questions about this again, and I really don't think that this is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem is that that part was not reviewed by the witness, that was the main problem, why we didn't put it. Mr. Ierace, what line --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is the line that begins with the word "before" in the paragraph that begins with the words "mainly that was the ammunition."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will read the whole paragraph to the witness. There is another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you were asked to quantify the ammunition bought from Yugoslavia, your answer reads upon the question "can you quantify it in tons or another measure?" Your answer was: "Mainly that was the ammunition for the -- for the infantry weapons. As far as I know, mostly for the 7.62 automatic rifle, and anti-aircraft cannons, 20 millimetres, that ammunition as well. That was before when I -- before I left for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the period between July and September 1994. Until before this period as far as I know ammunition was not supplied from other sources." Does that reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the very final part of your statement when the investigators told you that this would conclude the interview, you were asked whether you would like to add anything, and I read part of what you then added. You said: "Because the artillery weaponry that was taken out so to say on the Serb side was not taken out with a purpose to destroy Sarajevo. It was actually taken out to prevent the other side to get into possession of that, and it was used to protect everybody who was in possession of that. And for sure there was a lot of cases of discipline violations like it is in that kind of war." Does this reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP30 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the order of the sentence or something like that, that's what it says in English. You could say that that is how it was, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would. Thank you for these answers. Is there any further clarifications sought? If not, then I again would like to thank you for coming to The Hague. We all know it is a far distance and not only for answering the questions both of the parties and of Bench, but also for doing a lot of homework yesterday. The review of your statement took you a lot of time as the Chamber noticed. Thank you very much for that and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you perhaps please escort the next witness in the courtroom as well. We will attribute to the documents marked by the witness a provisional number, so that even at a later stage we have to decide on the admission of the whole lot of documents and tapes, that at least we have numbered these transcripts already. Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the English would be P3766A; and the B/C/S P3766.1A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would then be the provisional numbering for the transcript as they have been marked by the witness. No decision yet has been taken as to the admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but it should be clear that the Defence has an objection against this type of procedure and we will explain, if necessary, what it is when the Prosecution files these new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's specifically the reason why we said that this was a provisional number given to these documents. The Defence may --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one other exhibit from the previous witness, and that was the document shown by me to the witness during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can deal with that, but I would rather first try to finish with the witness and I noticed that there is still one document to be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Two documents, actually, the pseudonym sheet as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet as well. We will not forget that. Is the Defence ready to continue the examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when your examination was interrupted we stopped, I think, at the question of the Jewish cemetery, did you remember that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you told us that you yourself had dug trenches along the Jewish cemetery; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. The testimony was that he dug trenches below the Jewish cemetery, in fact he gave the term "at the transit road."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is of importance to be very precise in quoting to the witness what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I agree, but along that could be -- along in two directions. Very well. To save time, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly where you dug trenches in the direction of the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Muslim side by the Jewish cemetery, that is where I dug trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, we were talking about trenches. Were there any other military -- was there any other kind of military work that was carried out in the surroundings of the Jewish cemetery; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what kind of military work was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people who were digging there were involved in preparing facilities for the Muslim Army. These were the trenches in which they would keep weapons. So we dug into the depth and we made certain forms of cover so that they could be protected from bad weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any other kind of work carried out, apart from these open trenches; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I could just add something: Each building that had been destroyed, there were weapons on each building that had been destroyed directed towards Grbavica --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will interrupt you there. I am not -- I am only talking about the so-called Jewish cemetery area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I would like to, as you did not confront the witness with the literal text as I invited you to do. Yesterday you testified, Mr. DP2, and I will read your testimony literally. Upon the question: "Witness, could you tell us the names of the places where you dug?" Your answer was: "Yes, I dug on the Muslim side of the Jewish cemetery below the transit road." Is that -- that's the answer you gave yesterday. Is that a correct answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was by the Jewish cemetery itself, and I can say that we didn't only dig those trenches, but we also dug tunnels in the direction of the Jewish cemetery, a tunnel that the Muslim soldiers used to get to the following houses, to the cellars of those houses and I know that they dug trenches up until the chapel of the Jewish cemetery, and this was done usually at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned tunnels that had been dug, it seems in the direction of houses and what we call the chapel here. How did you obtain this information? What is the basis for your knowledge, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before digging, they would ask for volunteers to dig in that tunnel. These volunteers had to have boots because there was a lot of water in there. I really didn't volunteer at any time, and I didn't dig in the tunnel, but I do know that there were people who did dig there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you see these volunteers either digging tunnels or coming out once they had accomplished their work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you speak to any people who might have been involved in digging this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They said it was hard work, that digging was hard, so it was necessary to have special equipment to do this digging and as I said, I didn't have such equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How do you know that this tunnel went in the direction of the chapel, which is what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that because the soldiers that we spoke to told me that a tunnel was being dug in the direction or rather up to the chapel, and that soon they would reach the chapel and it would be possible to observe Grbavica with greater ease.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, we would like to provide -- we would like to show a couple of maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be better prepared, Mr. President, bearing in mind the various factors, when will we have the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect to have the next break at a quarter to 2.00, and just to inform the parties that I tried to arrange to continue at approximately 4.00, after another court session will be finished. After this other case will - which is a Status Conference - will have been finished, then we -- it will be half an hour break and then we will continue in courtroom I. I asked, as you are aware of, to see whether there would be a possibility for you to confer with General Galic in this same court building. We have not a final answer to that yet. So I expect that we will stop at a quarter to 2.00. And I have one additional question so that we get -- is it just a matter of the laptop to be brought with you when conferring with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing that I would like to have is to show everything to General Galic so that he can work for the end of the year, by the end of the year and organise his defence. Tomorrow that will be impossible. If we can do it later on in the courtroom, that would be perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not in control of what is brought in or not. If you need your laptop during the conversation, that's clear, we could see then whether this is allowed. If you would leave anything for General Galic, there might be -- in order to take with him to the Detention Unit, then, of course -- let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A conference in the courtroom is not possible. I don't know whether -- because the courtroom is -- all the courtrooms are used this afternoon, that's also why we had some difficulties in scheduling. But if it is just the laptop you want to bring during the conference, that would be -- permission will then be asked for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was another problem I was speaking about, but thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you had some time to look at this map. Do you recognise it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be able to get ahold of a black pen, please. And to draw accurately the locations where you were forced to dig these trenches.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is here from Unioninvest on the map, alongside the Jewish cemetery towards up here, that was the location of digging the trenches in this area. The second location I said that was on Mount Trebevic on a hill. It is approximately this location here. The Serbian Army was here on the road and we dug 50 metres below there. That's the second location. The third location is Faletici, this way, and north-east of Sarajevo, along the surface of the Borije hill, or I should say, Mountain Borije. And it goes just off the map here. So these were the locations of the trench digging during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, the witness indicated when he went to the north-east of the map, that the line would theoretically continue outside of the map for approximately the same distance in the direction of south-west off the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You just drew these four sites, so to speak, and could you tell us, but please don't mark anything yet, whether you were able to see, could you locate the chapel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chapel would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just point at it. Perhaps you could give the pointer to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a pointer that the witness could use? Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We will come back to that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I am not indicating anything because the pointer is too thick. We will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in the trenches that you've indicated, that you have marked, were you in a position to see active troops; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment. To the extent that you managed to see these troops, did you manage to see their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which weapons did you observe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic weapons, Kalashnikovs, machine-guns. On two locations I saw the so-called TG machine-guns, they were called the sowers of death. I saw grenades or shells of different calibres and different dimensions. And ordinary rifles. That would be all I saw on the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Each of the defenders of the soldiers that you saw, were they all armed; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you see -- and I am not speaking about light weapons, I am now speaking about heavy weapons -- did you see other heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the lines, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may point out, if I may interrupt, there is no reference to the time period as to whether this falls within the indictment period or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that the questions are about the period when the witness was digging trenches, and I think there is a time period known.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unless you would disagree with me, but I think the witness has stated when he first was rounded up and on a more regular basis -- but if it's not clear enough, then you could, of course, during cross-examination clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in fact. Yes, that was alternate rhythm, and we are speaking about the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what is a mortar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see any during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us where were you able to see such mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw mortars --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Don't, please, put the pen down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw mortars in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And on the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. When we are speaking about mortars, what were the mortars that you saw? Were they all the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. When we are speaking about the type of transport for the mortars, Witness, was there a difference, were some of these mortars, could they be characterised by a particular means of transport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Sarajevo, mortar and anti-aircraft machine-gun were on some kind of a car, and these were those vehicles, they were mobile, and from there fire was opened from the streets towards our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, in the English transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am sorry to interrupt, but it is not clear from the transcript as to which period the witness is referring to with regard to the digging of trenches. In fact, there is reference to beginning of the war in April and May, we were rounded up, and he goes on to say, but he does not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then perhaps we could clarify for the -- you told us when you were digging trenches, until when did this last? I mean, when did you stop being involved in digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stopped digging the trenches on the 8th of June 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's when you left Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are talking about mortars, you are referring to this whole period as well, so on from the beginning of the conflict until you left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I also think that our period this morning is finished. I wanted to ask the witness to point something on the map, but that may be for this afternoon, later this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps just one question to round this off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in the transcript when you gave the answer to my very last question, you mentioned a car, you mentioned an automobile. Thank you. Were you thinking of an automobile, a car, or some other vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a freight vehicle about 3 tons, we call it a van, a Kombi [phoen], a van. And this van, not just on one van, but on several vans there was a platform, a flatbed, the back, and as I said, there would be a mortar and a machine-gun and these vehicles would go from one street to the next and they would be firing on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is a good moment to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn. I will make a few remarks. The first one is that I did not see reflected in the transcript this morning, and it might have been out of the modesty, that the Chamber appreciated very much the work of the transcribers. So I hope it will now be in the transcript. Apart from that, arrangements are being prepared, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to have an opportunity to meet with General Galic between 2 and 4.00 in a room where you are allowed to bring your laptop in. I apologise, General Galic, for you, because it is a relatively long day and I know that this is asking a lot of you. I hope that you will have understanding that we would like to given the possibility for the witnesses to return and not to be forced to come back again. The schedule is that we in courtroom I at 3.00, a Status Conference starts. I take it that the Status Conference might take at least three quarters of an hour. We would then need half an hour break so that it will take us to 4.15. I cannot guarantee that we can start at 4.15, it might be later, but I would like to ask the parties to be ready at 4.15 to resume, and you, Mr. DP2, in order to make it possible for you to return home and not to have to come back again, we scheduled an additional hearing this afternoon so we hope to see you back at a quarter past 4.00. We will adjourn presumably until quarter past 4.00 or at a later time in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we are in a different courtroom, I'd like to ask Madam Registrar to call the case again, although we have been sitting this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. I'm glad to see that not only the parties and the witness, but also those who without whom we could not do our work are present and are assisting us. Madam usher, could you please escort the witness DP2 into the courtroom. The laptops are not working at this very moment. Madam usher, I think the curtains could be pulled up again. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, to continue with where we left off, what we need is to have the same map placed on the ELMO that we had before at just before the break of our hearing this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you will remember that at the end of the previous hearing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have no interpretation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the right interpretation in the language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there no interpretation at this moment? Could we see whether we are on the right channel, number 6? You now can hear us in a language you understand? Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it now. I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon again, Witness. You will remember that when we broke off this morning, you were telling us about the existence of mortars. You do remember, that don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke to us about these mortars that were mounted on what you called combis or vans. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How come do you know this? Have you seen it yourself with your own eyes, these vans, these combis, first question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I'd like to thank you for the time that you have made available for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you answer the question now, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the answer to your question is that yes, I have seen it with my own eyes. And not just me, any citizen of Sarajevo could have seen it who wanted to see it, who wanted to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you here. Did you see one such van, one such small lorry or more than one, several?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On every occasion that I saw them, I saw one of those. But there were two types. One would be a lorry from which there would be an anti-tank machine-gun that would fire from one of them. And then there would be a different type which would have a mortar that would be firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. How many people were there as crew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the van from which anti-tank machine-gun was fired, there would be just one person. And on the other type, there would be three crew members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask a question that could be relevant for both types of lorries. These crew members, were they dressed in uniforms, in civilian clothes, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're now going to go on to other mortars, the ones that I would call fixed mortars. Have you ever seen in Sarajevo mortars that seem to be established at fixed points inside the city? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For the Serb translation, for the -- not for the lines, for the city. So the fixed locations inside the city.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So could you have a look at the map which is to your left. And we're using a black pen. Could it please be checked, Madam, if it is a black pen. Could you indicate any such sights that you can remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just clarify something else in relation to these mortars, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is important. On every occasion, these mortars would appear in certain streets. In those circumstances where it was for people who were entering the city for various reasons, to show to these people a specific state of war, situation of war. What I mean to say is that we all knew inside the city that whenever there was parliamentarians from different states, from different countries, whether they were government representatives, journalists, reporters, cameramen, cultural workers, we would know that in the next day or in the days that would follow, there would be a mortar which would fire and provoke the Serb side in order to respond in fire, to return fire, so that these people could experience Sarajevo at war. And this is the absolute truth. And this is exclusively then that these mortars were used, were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for these clarifications. But what I wanted is if you could indicate for us, if you can, the locations from which you saw mortars fired.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the roundabout road, now it's the Street of Young Muslims, here in this location, I saw in one garden six mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please place a cross, a small cross, at this location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And next to it, could you please put number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in. It's difficult to look at it on the... But please, on where the witness marked and not on another place. Please a bit more upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the witness is asked to indicate the time period during which he saw these mortars at these particular positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness could do so. May I ask you, Mr. DP2, Mr. DP2, whenever your answer is about a period which is not between September 1992 and the date you left Sarajevo, would you please indicate if it would be earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that I am saying, it relates to the time when I was in Sarajevo until the 9th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to this location, you told us about a garden next to this site. Were there monuments, one, or more monuments that may have had a historical or cultural or religious-type monuments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where the mortars were placed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: At location 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a garden, garden of a private house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now indicate to us other locations where, to your knowledge, you saw such weapons placed. Could you place a cross and next to it, number 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the position quite close to the Markale market opposite the academy of music in front of a kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the kindergarten, I saw two mortars placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you describe these mortars, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A long barrel. It has a fixed base, a platform. On the side, there are two legs. And on the side, there is an instrument for correcting the level, for adjusting the level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see any ammunition together with the batteries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The crew serving the batteries --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I saw that passing by. So it could have been just 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Wait for my question, please. The crews serving the batteries, how were they dressed? Civilian clothes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has not referred to crews in these particular questions. The Defence counsel is leading the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I wonder --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You interrupted when -- Mr. DP2, when you said you saw it only passing by, what actually did you mean? You talked about 15 seconds. What would you see during this 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just saw two mortars and no one else. There was no one else around these two mortars at that moment when I was passing by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were fixed mortars in a fixed position, or were they mounted on vans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, they were fixed on the ground. I said in front of the kindergarten, and now in the place of that kindergarten, it's the Holy See embassy now. It used to be a kindergarten. But that's where it was on the ground. They were fixed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was no one near to that, no mortar crew, soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Just alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please continue to do the same.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also saw two mortars in front of the museum of the Winter Olympic Games. And that was the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And if you can put a cross and a number 3 next to it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these mortars of the same type, the same kind of mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same mortars, and also there were no crews around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please continue with the same exercise.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Furthermore, I saw mortars in the area of the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade led by Commander Caco. When I was a hostage I saw that in that area of a very large compound where there were weapons. I saw several mortars there. I don't know whether there were more than two. I don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us where the location is with a cross and place number 4 next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And perhaps the picture could be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I couldn't see where the witness was marking because... Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are there any other locations where you saw such batteries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I will now change the subject. You have told us under number 4 that there was the headquarters of Caco. What can you tell us on the subject of the weapons that you were perhaps able to see there, and not only heavy weapons but other weapons including ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that very large room, apart from the mortars, I saw many grenades or shells of different sizes, different calibres. I saw dozens and dozens of handguns. I saw Kalashnikov automatic rifles. I saw ordinary rifles. And I think that would be all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us to which period does this relate to, your observations relate to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that precisely on the 28th of October 1993, during the clash or the showdown between the police and Caco that night when Caco was killed. I was a hostage then, and I told you about this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The weapons that you were able to see, did they seem to be old to you, ancient, or rather, new weapons, recent weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the army. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now, I'd like us to change the subject. And could we examine some other matters as well. First of all, have you ever heard that there was firing in the city, that is, from the city, was there firing from heavy weapons from inside the city? And I include mortars in the heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I said is that I heard that, and since I live on the fourth floor, and from my windows I can see the panorama of Sarajevo, I was following the range. And this shell, when it was fired, landed on the police centre, that is, on the special police centre of Dragan Vikic. I didn't hear, but a friend who lives near these two checkpoints, near these two locations, these two sites of mortars, he told me that these two places were hit from the Serb side, and that these four mortars were destroyed. That is, in front of the kindergarten and in front of the Museum of the Winter Olympic Games. I can also give the name of my friend and professor. If it is necessary, I can give his name in writing because he lives nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Possibly it may happen that we will go into closed session. It is possible, but we may do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to go in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. We could go into private session. I think it would be enough, because then the words spoken will not go to the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke to us about a school, a children's school. Can you tell us the name of that school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was a kindergarten, a kindergarten. I don't know what the name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Perhaps the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's at the beginning of Logavina Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you're speaking of the schools now, what can you tell us about what happened to the schools during the war to your knowledge, personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that primary schools, secondary schools, kindergartens, and faculties were used as military facilities. Above Caco's headquarters, 200 metres from there, and his headquarters was just 5 metres above former military command of General Kukanjac. And during the war, that was the Egyptian SFOR forces. So his command was some 10 metres above. I don't know -- it was a school. I don't know what the name was, but it was a primary school, and there were kitchens there. And also soldiers' rooms. And behind that school, I went to dig the trenches. So every morning, we would have breakfast there, and I know that because I was there every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since your answer was very long, could I please summarise your testimony in the following way: You say that you saw several schools that were reused by the army in order to provide accommodation for the troops, location -- premises of the troops. Is that how I should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now, can we go back to the questions of shelling, shellings, mortar shellings. To your knowledge, were there any particular circumstances that surrounded the beginning of shelling in Sarajevo, the shelling operations that were coming from the city itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean mortar provocation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I don't know. It's up to you to say that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were lorries with anti-aircraft machine-guns. And -- I apologise. With mortars mounted on the van. And I said that they had to do with provocations in the sense that they would go out into the street and they would fire, they would always fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will interrupt you there. When there were firing operations or when there were going to be, when there was going to be shelling, I'm talking about shelling, were any protective measures taken in the town in order to protect the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's clearer to me now. There were no measures taken to inform and protect the population. I know very well that the population included women, went out into the street very often, and they prevented mortars from firing from their streets because a consequence would always be that a window would be shattered or a roof would be destroyed. So citizens protested. They didn't want these mortars to be used because they didn't want return -- they didn't want shelling in response to cause damage. And this didn't happen only on one occasion; this happened quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to go back to another object, what we call the old brewery, Pivara. Are you familiar with this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this place is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Tell us, tell us. Don't show it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you tell us about this place at the time that you experienced the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brewery was a place whether the citizens of Sarajevo were provided with water, supplied with water. There was a long pipe that been installed in front of the brewery, and there were about 20 taps from which the citizens could collect water. They went there to collect water. And one street further up, we always waited in a queue for bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know whether what we call the brewery had certain installations within it?
