utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said there were rumours according to which certain weapons were being produced in the brewery. Similarly, they said that that was being done in the school at the other end the town that is called Vaso Miskin Crni.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now please take the same black felt tip that you used a minute ago and mark where this last place that you mentioned is located on the map. If the technical booth could focus on the image.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, next to that cross -- just a minute. Just a minute, please. I see that we have two maps. No. Mark that place with the number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you tell us what was produced in this technical factory? But first of all, where did you obtain the information that you have about it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were rumours. This is something I was told.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness didn't refer to a technical factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer of the witness that he knows about it on the basis of rumours. This asks for speculation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So please proceed, but not on the basis of rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. There's just one question that I would nevertheless like to ask, and it's whether these rumours were known at the time of the war. May I have your permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as such -- I mean, they are not any less rumours. But if you want to know whether the witness was aware of the rumours that exist during the war or after the war, it's fine. But it doesn't take away the character of rumours to the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Mr. President. But many rumours make more noise than just one rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you answer this question, please. When did you become aware of what you have called rumours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I found out about this in 1993. But at this point I would like to say that what I saw confirmed these rumours, what I saw when I was returning from digging trenches. Down at Miljacka, they were experimenting with the results of the production of weapons in Sarajevo, they were trying this out. I then saw a sort of platform, and there was some kind of a machine-gun on that platform. There were two soldiers in camouflage uniform, and they put a rifle-launched grenade at the front. They removed -- they moved back. They pulled a wire that been connected to it. It exploded. It flew away very far, and they congratulated each other. So the hypothesis according to which there really was production in Sarajevo is correct. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you how you know that these people who were trying out shots and that they weren't firing at a real target?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a zone where the BH Army was active, and the Serbian positions were far away. And the place where the shell was fired and the place where it fell, well, the distance between these two places was about 300 metres. So not more than that. And this was all in the Miljacka canyon. This was just a test.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you say what the name was, the name that we see in the transcript, the name of this place. Could you tell us whether you can see it on the map? Witness, can it be seen on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark it with a cross and a circle, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say exactly, but it was in the autumn of 1993. Either in September or October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: For the purpose of the transcript, the witness has marked -- there's a cross and placed the figure 6 there. That's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the figure 6 is added by the witness. Before continuing, I would wonder, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and I'm also addressing the Prosecution, the Chamber would very much appreciate if it could finish with this witness today. It would otherwise be a very long interruption for just a very short time. How much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much more time, Mr. President. I'll confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half an hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that we could not finish today, because then it would be 5 minutes to 6.00. We would then have a break of 20 minutes, and three quarters of an hour would be left for the Prosecution which would not be fair. How much time does the Prosecution think it would need for the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, several very significant issues have been raised through this witness. And most of it has not been covered in the 65 ter summary, in addition to which those are questions which have not been put to the Prosecution witnesses in breach of Rule 90(h). Especially with regard to the question of mortars, mobile mortars, and there are certain issues that really go to the root of the Prosecution evidence, so we would require to perhaps investigate into these. And therefore, at this stage, Mr. President, I cannot guarantee that I could finish within the time period left tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in view of many circumstances, also in view of the 65 ter summary, the Chamber thinks that you should finish in -- within 15 minutes. We'll then see how far we come with the Prosecution, and we'll see after cross-examination has started. And at 7.00, because we'll not go one single minute beyond 7.00. We'll see whether there's any need, necessity, to recall the witness at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to make an observation that we have asked three hours for this witness. We've only used up one and a half hours, and we lost much time this morning that were not our fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Half hour, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But apart from that, I was also referring to the 65 ter summary. You went on many subjects that are not clearly, as far as I can see, in the 65 ter summary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, bearing in mind the time constraints, could you please answer with a yes or no as much as you can. Do you know about the existence of other military targets in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please briefly tell us which other targets that could be described as military you're thinking of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many schools, kindergartens where troops were stationed, troops of the BH Army of the 1st Corps. The 1st Mountain, 10th Brigade. 10th Mountain and many other locations where troops were stationed. So I would that following the mobilisation in May 1992, the entire Sarajevo was divided into people who were troops and people who were working for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to ask you a question. Tanks that were also military targets, can you tell us whether there were one or more tanks in the city of Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have seen some tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. How many tanks have you seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How many have you seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the tunnel of Ciglane and near the engineering school, engineering faculty and architecture faculty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What else was near what we call the technical faculty? Which other establishment was near? Where is the technical faculty, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way to the Kosevo stadium towards the faculty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be required to state when the tanks were observed by him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I instructed the witness to tell us if it was outside the period September 1992 until the moment when he left Sarajevo. So may I take that you saw these tanks within this time period I gave to you before? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really only speaking about the time that I was in Sarajevo until the 9th of June, 1994. I am speaking about what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but also, please keep in mind that we are not talking about the period on from the beginning of the conflict, but that we are specifically interested to know from September 1992 until, as you said, the moment when you left Sarajevo. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, just one thing, that has how been two or three times we have had the same objection regarding the time frame. I think the witness has understood. I think we have all understood, and I would like to ask the Prosecution not to interrupt. Perhaps for other things, but not for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where is the faculty that you have called--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason for this is the Prosecution is entitled to more information than that. The period the witness is referring to is from the beginning of 1992 to June 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can ask the witness in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, where was the technical faculty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a technical faculty. It's an engineering faculty. It is located opposite the tunnel called Ciglane. That's where there's a market, and opposite there's an Orthodox and Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd like you to place some crosses, that is, from number 7 onwards, in relation to the locations that you have just mentioned, that is, the faculty, the Ciglane tunnel, and I believe the third location being...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, earlier, you spoke of the brewery. Do you know if this brewery was ever systematically shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "no," you say that it has not been shelled? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of Bistrik was never shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, now I'd like us to go back to the question of the trenches. You dug trenches. Do you know how many successive lines did the BH Army have, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strategy of the Army of BH was to have -- the closer they were to the Serbs the better it was to attack. In Borije we had even three lines of trenches, and in some cases there were two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know how were these trenches connected to each other, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were connected to go from one trench to another. There were these channels that were connecting the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you know what the transporter is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity of seeing any in the city of Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of seeing an improvised transporter that was made of a lorry. It was made of a lorry, and it had a very small window to see through, if that was a transporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Can you tell us briefly what happened, to your knowledge, in February 1992? We are speaking about the period before the official breakout of the war. What were you able to see very briefly in Sarajevo during this period in February 1992? And after that, I'll only have one more question, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I lived in February and March, there were lively activities to do with the barracks of the JNA. Snipers went up the building, to my building. They were going up on the roof and around. I saw a machine-gun nest. There were Green Berets. And they were observing the troops of the JNA. On the road going towards my work of employment, to Hidrogradnja, which is a building of my company, from that building, I saw people in camouflage uniforms leaving that building with Zoljas, armed with Zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You're speaking about the uniforms. No, I'll withdraw that. What was the period that you saw this, when you saw this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in February, March -- before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Were you ever in a bread line, in a bread queue, what was known as a bread queue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you ever subjected to shelling while you were doing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. There was only in Vaso Miskin Crni Street, I was there in the bread queue. Although that is a different subject and I could go on and speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why is that a separate subject? Can you tell us very briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Vaso Miskin Street was really a turning point in the war, and the relationship in the war, because the relationship of the sides in the war because many civilians died there and because the Serb side was blamed for causing the massacre. And there could be evidence that could be brought that this wasn't the case, that this wasn't like it seemed, since I was a participant in the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What is your personal feeling? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a feeling; it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: He is inviting the witness to speculate and give an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness in the beginning of his answer says that he wants to answer. He was asked about feelings, to give an answer about facts. Could you tell us what fact you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before this event, throughout the time we received the bread, in front of the cinema Romanija, we waited for the bread in a sheltered passage, in a corridor, in a hallway. And on that day, when the massacre occurred, we were taken to the street of Vaso Miskin Crni Street. This street is facing the Serb positions so that a shell which could possibly fall would be attributed to having come from the Serb side. I have information from the 1st Mountain Brigade that this was done by the Muslims, that they were shelling -- that they shelled, they launched the grenade from Planika. That the person who had launched the grenade was killed by a sniper, and that the sniper, marksman had been killed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Are you telling about what you heard from other persons? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard this from a soldier, a BH Army soldier who was not -- who was in the 1st Mountain Brigade, who had received the very first Golden Lily Medal from the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I'd like to have his parents' names protected, and his name. It's a very delicate matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us before that you had only one question left. Since then I heard some three questions, and a quarter of an hour is over as well, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only wanted, if I may, to ask two more questions and submit a document to the witness. We were taken a little by surprise. We have the document here. It can be distributed, with your leave, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the document is ready, it could not have been such a surprise. Yes, but this certainly will lead to a situation where we should allow the Prosecution to recall the witness. So please proceed. But try to see what we can do. Two questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. One question you indicated became three questions. These two questions are really two questions and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since I have only one questions I am going to put to you, I have two questions to put to you and I'm going to put those questions to you. On the basis of on your personal experience of the fighting, in general terms, what were the targets shelled by the Serbian forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically, I can say that the response was always such that when there was a provocation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to interrupt you. What do you know about the targets that were shelled by the Serbian forces in Sarajevo? My question is, as a general rule, what was the nature of these targets, if you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was responsed to fire from Sarajevo, and targeted the targets from which they were active.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on the basis of the document that you have to the right of you or in front of you, I don't know where it has been placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could put it on the ELMO. Thank you. No, we're in private session, so please take it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are not in private session. We are in open session, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So we need a redaction for that. And we now return into closed session, perhaps that's needed for the ELMO. It's not just -- no, if it's not on the ELMO, then we could deal with it in private session. If we can do without the ELMO, then it would save us pulling down the curtains and opening them again. So if private session would do, we now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber was informed that when the witness was brought in, that conversations took place in a language that could be understood by the witness between the Defence counsel and General Galic. That's the reason why I asked the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom again. It should be clear by now that there should be no conversations that could be heard by a witness during his presence in this courtroom. And whether you exchange seasons greetings or whatever, it's uncontrollable and therefore at several occasions we indicated clearly that it was not permitted. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just a technical problem that the General and his counsel were interested in. And has nothing to do with the case, absolutely. You can be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will gladly accept that. But as you also know, it's uncontrollable. If you want to exchange whatever information with General Galic, you should do it at such a level of sound that it could not be heard by the witness. Ms. Mahindaratne. Is it you or is it Mr. Ierace who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is Ms. Mahindaratne -- might I just explain that for technical reasons, the sound from the courtroom is not being broadcast outside. This witness has given a lot of evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just see. At this moment, we are in open session. Is that what you meant? I didn't understand you quite well, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are at this moment in open session. I don't know whether you refer to the present situation in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, I refer to the times that we are in open session, Mr. President. None of the sound is being heard elsewhere in the OTP. So it's not possible for the Prosecution team to do any reasonable preparation in relation to this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So as to enable us to properly cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did this last, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Throughout this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why were we not informed at an earlier stage? So that we could have seen -- we were. I see that Madam Registrar informs me that at least someone in this courtroom was aware. I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the sound in almost all of the building was normally functioning, but that in the hall as far as I understand, that there was a delay of 30 minutes. But I do understand that this caused you problems. My question would be, would you be ready to start to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We are ready to start, but we certainly won't finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's see how far we come. Would you please try to prioritise as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, we prepared it that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I please proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the map D1897 [sic], I believe, the map that was shown to the witness during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's 1817, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you marked on this map with figure 1 a place where you claim to have seen six mortars in a garden.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many times did you see these six mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least five or six times. Whenever I returned from digging the trenches in the Jewish cemetery by the Mladih Muslimana Street to my flat. So, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give the precise date. And if you cannot remember the date, perhaps the month and the year, when you saw these six mortars for the first time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1993. August, September, October.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, my question was the first time you saw it, so are you saying it could be either August, September, or October, or are you saying that you saw these mortars during this period, August, September, October 1993? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to this conclusion on the basis of the fact that this street earlier on in 1992 -- I never went down this street before. I went down to -- went down the flat part, and only in 1993 I had the courage to go down that street. That's why I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say you had the courage to go down there, does it mean that you went down there to see these mortars or you visited that area? How did you come across these mortars? Can you please explain the circumstances under which you saw these mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see in this map, that is the shortest route to my flat. I saw it by chance on the way to my flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said before 1993, you did not have courage to go down there. Does it mean that during that period, you took a different route?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a very wide route. It was empty, and it was very open, so you really had to be courageous to go down that road. Earlier on, I always took a different route.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, could you explain what you mean by "courage"? Why did you require "courage" to go down there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps courage is a term which is too strong. But if the road is open in the direction of Trebevic, in the direction of all the other centres, it's a lot safer to go through the houses rather than to take a road which is open, which is exposed. So perhaps it's not a matter of courage, but there is a risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So what do you mean by risk? What type of risk would you face if you did take that route where it should be open to Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a well-known fact that there was sniper fire in Sarajevo, and to tell you the truth, I was afraid of sniper fire. And perhaps of a shell that gone astray.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So is it your position that if one took that route, you could be exposed to sniper fire, and are you saying from which direction one could anticipate sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I was fired at by a sniper in my flat I could expect the same to happen there because if I may say so, I'm not a citizen of the town of Sarajevo who is not well-known.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, my question was at that position which you've marked with a figure 1, you said there was a threat of sniper fire, of being exposed to sniper fire there. From which direction? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all directions. The right bank of the Miljacka, because this transit road can't be seen from the Serbian positions, or it's almost impossible to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I did not ask you as to what positions, whether it was open to Serb positions. My question to you was as to what direction could one anticipate sniper fire. Let me put it to you, sir, you stated that this location was open to Trebevic. Your words were "perhaps courage is a term which is too strong, but if the road is open in the direction of Trebevic, in the direction rather than to take a road which is open, which is exposed." Referring to Trebevic, what did you mean? Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said "open in the direction of Trebevic" then that was a mistake, and I withdraw that. I didn't say it was open in the direction of Trebevic because it can barely be seen from Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel switch off her microphone while the witness is answering the question, please. There is interference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you having difficulty with that particular question in trying to withdraw where you stated that the position is open to Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No difficulties, really. As I say, it's not open in the direction of Trebevic. And I said that it wasn't easy to see it from Trebevic. I don't see why you are insisting on this, because you probably want me to say that I was afraid of shells coming from Trebevic. But in my prior testimony, I kept repeating that they shot from Trebevic mostly when the Serbs were provoked. And that is when they shelled the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, during the period 1992 to the time you were in Sarajevo, that is, June 1994, did you visit Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apart from the fact that I went from when I was taken to dig trenches, but that's not Trebevic. Those are the slopes of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is you never went to Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war? No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In view of that answer, sir, how do you explain your response that this position where you marked as -- with figure 1 was not exposed to Trebevic? You said one could not see this place from Trebevic. How do you know if you never visited Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, this place, number 1 is on the side of a valley, and at the top, there is a house. This place can't be seen from either side, from any side, unless you really come close to that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you stated that you saw six mortars at the garden where you marked with figure 1, from where did you see it? Did you see it from the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was this road used by other civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. At that point I didn't see anyone on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about at that point, sir. Was this a road which was used other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you used the word "the road," you saw it from the road, isn't that the arterial road that goes by that location? Isn't that a main road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the main road. And as you see, it's not the Mladih Muslimana Road. That is the transit road that was made when we had the Winter Olympics. It goes around Sarajevo. It's on the route from Sarajevo to Belgrade. It's the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is the route one has to take if one were to go to Bistrik. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the roads at the foot of Trebevic, but there are other roads that go to Bistrik. This can be seen on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your position is that one could see these six mortars from that road? That is your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: During the period, and you refer to the period September, October 1993, did you see these mortars fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anyone by these mortars. I only saw the mortars that had been mounted on that slope in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is there any identifying features of this house, or do you know what that house was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- it was a house upstairs, and below, in the garden, there were the six mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that house occupied by some persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it an abandoned house or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was intact. Nothing was missing. But I didn't see anyone in the house or outside the house either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is there any particular feature about that house which could be used to guide one to this particular house which could help one to identify this house again? Could you perhaps describe some identifying feature of this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A house with four walls made of bricks. But if some sort of evidence is really necessary, I can photograph that place and send you the photograph. That really isn't a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony was that you saw two mortars fixed at the kindergarten. You marked this with figure 2 on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Exactly when did you see these mortars? And I'm asking you about the month and the year, if you do not remember the date.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to mention the day and the year, too. But I could say that it was also in the winter in 1993. But this is just a rough guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How many times did you see these two mortars at this particular location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on one occasion. Because there was no reason for me to move around those parts of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That was a time, you said, it was just 15 seconds, you just passed through this place within 15 seconds. That was the time you saw these two mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If I had to pass by a building, I think that's the amount of time it took.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were going on that particular day when you saw these two mortars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to see a friend whom I have mentioned here under protective measures. He lives 50 metres from that kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with [Realtime transcript omitted in error] weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I didn't have any, I obtained some during the war. I wasn't in the army, but I can distinguish between an automatic rifle and a rifle and a mortar and a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, for the sake of the transcript, could one specify what is missing at line 12, page 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I used the word "weaponry."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that within 15 minutes -- 15 seconds, I beg your pardon, you recognised two mortars positioned at the location you identified with figure 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than that even.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In your testimony, you stated that you saw mortars close to the Markale market. Is that the place you indicated with figure 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This place is as far away from Markale as the location under number 3, about 150 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate on the map with the pointer --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps the map could be placed on the ELMO and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the map may be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, could you please place the pointer on the exact location of Markale market.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What pen is the witness using at this very moment? A black one, yes. It should have been a blue one. When examined by the Prosecution, we use a different colour. The witness marks the map just below right the number 3 with a circle and a cross. That was the marking made on the request of the Prosecution. So it should be have been in blue. Could you please circle again around the circle to add a blue line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Markale market is in Marsala Tito Street, and right next to it is the tram station that I've indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, when did you see the mortars you indicated you saw at the position you marked with figure 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was in winter, December, January 1993. I mean, that is approximately. I could be mistaken, approximately, that time. I don't recall. It was a long time ago. But I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position, sir, that you saw the two mortars at the location marked with figure 2? And the two mortars you saw at the location marked with figure 3 during winter 1993? Is it your position that you saw mortars at both these locations during the same period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps there was a pause of about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a chronological objection. When we're saying "winter 1993" we never know whether it's winter 1992/1993 or winter 1993/1994. Could we make this precise, and this is also valid for what the witness said earlier. He spoke of December, January 1993. I'm not quite sure that everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand your answer well, Mr. DP2, that when you're talking about December, January 1993, you're talking about December 1992 until January 1993? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that's December, January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be December 1992, January 1993? Is that how I have to understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So how many times did you see the mortars at the location marked with figure 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also only once. Also passing by, just like when I saw the mortars on the 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that also very briefly, within 15 seconds perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. While I was passing by.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe what the location number 2 is. Is it a building? Is it -- you said it's a kindergarten. What did it -- what does it look like? Can you describe the topography and the area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, it was a kindergarten, or a preschool, whatever --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry. I have to interrupt you, sir. I'm merely asking you to describe that particular area, what does it look like? At number 2, is there a building, are there several buildings? Is it a built up area? Could you just describe that area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The kindergarten there was there, and there was a low, one-storey building. A little bit in front of that, there was a yard. And in that yard were these two mortars under number 3. And there was a Museum of the Winter Olympic Games that had three storeys. And in front of it, there was the courtyard with the figure of a skier, and there were two mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the yard at the kindergarten where the mortars were located, is it by the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the right-hand side of the road. As I'm coming down Bjelave on the right-hand side, if I'm going up, then it's on the left-hand side. Now at this location as I said is the embassy of the Holy See. That is the location. At the moment, there is no kindergarten there. It's the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What's the name of that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that's Logavina Street, but I may be mistaken. But I can look it up on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's not necessary, Witness. Witness, if I may interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was this road used by other civilians, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the road that is used. It's a town street. It's a public road for all the citizens that need to go to Bjelave, to that part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen UN vehicular traffic on that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a very good road. It's very, very steep, and it's not good for cars. That means it's -- it can be used, but not for cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So my question was not the condition of the road, as to whether you've seen UN vehicular traffic. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen UN vehicular traffic in Sarajevo, during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you still remember where you saw UN vehicles in Sarajevo during the time 1992 to June 1994 while you were there? Do you still remember and at what locations you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there is no part of town where I went without transporters, without humanitarian aid vehicles, without UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, the compound of the olympic -- Winter Olympic Museum in which you saw two mortars, is there a road going by that compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this road goes off to the left towards Markale. And by steep stairs, gets to the tram track.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that a public road which is used by civilians apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you describe that as a busy road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Not a main road, not that busy. There are only two very busy streets in Sarajevo. Titova Street and JNA Street. The rest are not so busy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do vehicles go on that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen UN vehicles passing through that road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember all the roads on which you haven't seen UN vehicles passing through during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, like all other the citizens of Sarajevo, I didn't move about town much. My location was the centre. And that other part where Caco was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Why didn't you move too much during the war while you were in Sarajevo? What was the reason for the restriction of your movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you won't believe this, but the reason was that we didn't have food. So I spent more time lying down than anything else, when I wasn't digging. I had two work obligations, and only when I had to go and to pick some medicinal herbs in order to make medicinal teas, herbal teas, I wouldn't go very much around the town. I would just go and pick these herbs, and I would spend the rest at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the distance from location marked number 2 to Markale market?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said about 150 to 200 metres in my assessment. Not more than that. As the crow flies, that would be the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what was the distance between location marked number 3 to Markale market?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also I answered that. The same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are there --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly there is a little further away, number 2, than number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Are there any other public institutions or places for public interest, markets, or public buildings near location marked 2 or 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a large building of PoljoOprema where Green Berets were stationed with the commander, chief of municipality of Stari Grad, a man called Hadzi Bajric. Also the Picadilly restaurant --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm asking for public buildings, not military buildings. I'm asking for public such as markets or such places around that area. Post offices, public buildings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Academy of music. And as I said, that company PoljoOprema, and down there, there are some shops.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you identified these locations, you yourself, without any prompting, used the word "these two locations are close to Markale market." What made you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. It's just that everyone knows about Markale market. And in order for people to orientate themselves, as a reference point; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is it your position that every aspect you identified in that area you identified in reference to Markale market? Is that your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is very general in relation to other facilities that the witness may have mentioned in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's how the question was meant to be. Do I understand you well, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My question was whether he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meant to be that broad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not inadmissible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness has not responded to my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Yes, I will. I believe that in that part of town, there isn't anything as recognisable as striking as the Markale market. That's the only reason why I mentioned that these locations were close to Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you saw several mortars at the location you identified with figure 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said that you saw these mortars in a large room. That was the testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your testimony was that this was the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP2 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have close contact with the 10th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, before the witness answers, we may have a problem of what kind of session we need, whether open or closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know how to say that without being too open. There are perhaps geographical reasons that we may need to switch.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interest of the time factor, we could perhaps go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into closed session. I wonder whether it's necessary or not. Private session would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me first address about Mr. -- Mr. DP2. Perhaps the witness should not be present during all the other things we have to discuss. Mr. DP2, as you might have noticed, the counsel for the Prosecution are taking the position that they have not yet finished your cross-examination. Since we are not sitting tomorrow and not until Christmas, if the Chamber would agree with the Prosecution, that would mean that we have to ask you to come back at a later stage. That would not be until somewhere in January. First of all, would you be available to come back if the Chamber would decide that further examination is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then would you please take care, first of all, that the place where you can be reached is available to the victims and witness unit so that they can approach you for a possible return into this courtroom. The second issue is that although it's for a long time, you're instructed not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given until now in this Court and not about the testimony you still are about to give in this Court. So speak with no one about your testimony until now and testimony still to come if any. May I then ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the transcript, could you please indicate what was the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I do not think that my learned colleague spoke about mobile telephones, perhaps it's because it's the end of the session, but we see that it says mobile telephones in the transcript. And I don't think this witness spoke of mobile telephones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... If the witness would return then the question whether or not about mobile telephones will be put to the witness again. Then, I would first of all for the sake of the transcript I earlier indicated that a redaction could be made. If the blinds could be drawn up again. I don't know if there's anyone who could push the button. If I could ask even for the assistance of the... If despite the noise you can still hear me, I indicated before that a redaction would be made in respect of the document D1818 having been on the ELMO. We have been informed by the technical booth that no image left ever this courtroom with exhibit D1818 on the ELMO. So the redaction will finally not be made. Then I'd like to address the Defence in respect of the following: The Defence has asked for four witnesses appearing on the initial list of witnesses to be replaced by four other witnesses. The Chamber wonders whether the replacement of the witness which appears under number 55 by another witness by the name of Krak would be justified, because we see that the summary of the testimony expected from Witness Number 55 is long and contains a lot of detail on various subjects, whereas the summary provided for the witness who would replace him is of a very general nature, and as far as we can see now, would not add substantially to the testimony of other witnesses. Therefore, the Defence should prepare for being allowed to call three witnesses instead of the four; but at the same time, the Defence still has an opportunity to give a short written submission in order to explain why the witness that would replace Witness Number 55 would be necessary, what would be the added value of that witness in respect of the other witnesses already called on this subject. So therefore, the Defence should be prepared that they will only be allowed to call three instead of four witnesses, and then for a total number of hours of six, then, instead of the eight scheduled. I further inform the parties that my account goes until, I think the day before yesterday, that the Prosecution took less time to cross-examine the witnesses as the Defence did in examining the witnesses in chief. I'm mentioning this because when the Defence cross-examined the Prosecution witnesses, they took more time than the Prosecution took in examination-in-chief. Now, we see the opposite picture. That is, the Defence using more time for the examination-in-chief than the Prosecution does in cross-examination. The Chamber will consider what should be the consequences of that, because it could finally result in considerably more time taken by one of the parties compared to the time taken by the other party. But we'll have to consider this in more detail, and we'll do this in due course. Is there any urgent matter apart from that I take it that the Defence would -- that the Prosecution would like to recall Witness DP2 in order to finish its cross-examination? Is there any other urgent matter that we have to deal with at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to the exhibits to be tendered through the witnesses to be called from the 8th of January, when we might expect notice or at least by which date the Defence should give us notice of those exhibits. I would be grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you could tell the Prosecution when they can expect your information, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll do whatever we can, Mr. President. But first of all, I wanted to ask you, could you bear in mind about our determination about the 6th of the current [sic]? I don't know whether you want any further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About the 6th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question for witnesses, Ukrainian Russian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Would have to be prepared for being allowed to call three rather than four witnesses. I'm talking about Ukrainian Russian witnesses, and we compared the summaries. And as I indicated before, especially in respect of Witness 55, which gives a lengthy summary, at least a lot of details, whereas the witness to replace him gives only general information rather than such detail and to some extent would be -- seems to be repetitious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take the wisest thing to do would be to prepare for the three most important witnesses, and then we'll see whether a fourth would be granted. If you would like to draw additionally attention to aspects not mentioned until now, you could do that. But then please do it on very short notice. Apart from that, I understand that you have been expressly invited to ask for -- timely ask for interpreters to be present so that we could examine these witnesses, and the registry informs me that no steps have been taken in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just looking. I think that the lady who was in charge has been informed, the person that we are supposed to be in touch with. That was on the 4th of December. There was a request addressed to Mrs. Matesic. And we have asked for the 8th, 9th, and 10th, January, interpreter for Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to know that it has been done. I think the registry asked for a confirmation of that. But I take it then, Ms. Pilipovic, that it has been done at a time well in advance of the appearance of these witnesses. Is there any other issue? Then, I first would like to thank especially the interpreters and the technical assistants who really did more than one could expect from someone. This is the last session before Christmas. Whether you celebrate Christmas in December or early in January, and whether you do it under the circumstances everyone would like to celebrate Christmas or under less favourable circumstances, as the Chamber is aware of that especially you, General Galic, that will be your situation, at least I wish you whatever you expect to find during the Christmas days and for the new year. We adjourn until the 8th of January. But it's not sure yet whether this will be in the morning or the afternoon, so I'd like to invite the parties to keep themselves acquainted with the Court schedule to be made public. We'll adjourn until the 8th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
